title: Palindrome Removal
statement: You are given an integer array `arr`. A move picks a contiguous, non-empty block `arr[i..j]` that is a palindrome (it reads the same from both ends; a single element always qualifies) and deletes it, after which the elements on its two sides become neighbours. Return the smallest number of moves that deletes every element of `arr`.
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every palindrome to delete, then recursing on what is left, explores an exponential number of arrays. Instead, think about the first element `arr[i]` of a range. Either it is deleted on its own, or it leaves in the same move as some later equal element `arr[k]`. In the second case everything strictly between them must be cleared first, and the very last of those moves can be widened to include `arr[i]` and `arr[k]` for free, because wrapping a palindrome in two equal values keeps it a palindrome. That splits the range into two independent smaller ranges, which is exactly interval DP.

## Approach

1. Let `dp[i][j]` be the fewest moves that clear `arr[i..j]`; an empty range costs 0.
2. Fill rows from `i = n - 1` down to 0 and, in each, `j` from `i` upwards, so smaller ranges are ready.
3. Start with `best = 1 + dp[i + 1][j]`: delete `arr[i]` alone.
4. If `arr[i]` equals `arr[i + 1]`, the pair is one move: `1 + dp[i + 2][j]`.
5. For each `k >= i + 2` with `arr[k] === arr[i]`, use `dp[i + 1][k - 1] + dp[k + 1][j]`: the pair rides along with the inside's last move.
6. Store `best` and return `dp[0][n - 1]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`arr = [1, 2]`. Row `i = 1`: `dp[1][1] = 1 + 0 = 1`. Row `i = 0`: `dp[0][0] = 1`; for `dp[0][1]`, `best = 1 + dp[1][1] = 2`, the neighbours `1` and `2` differ, and there is no `k`, so the answer is `2`. (In Example 2, matching the two `1`s gives `dp[1][2] + dp[4][4] = 2 + 1 = 3`.)

## Complexity

- Time: O(n³): O(n²) ranges, each scanning up to n split points.
- Space: O(n²) for the table.

## Pitfalls

- An adjacent equal pair (`k = i + 1`) has an empty inside, so it costs 1 move, not 0; handle it separately.
- Matching `arr[i]` with `arr[k]` only pays off together with the inside's last move; never add an extra move for it.
- Fill `i` downwards: `dp[i][j]` reads rows `i + 1` and beyond.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `arr` |
| `dp[i][j]` | fewest moves to clear `arr[i..j]` (0 when empty) |
| `i`, `j` | ends of the current range |
| `k` | a later position whose value equals `arr[i]` |
| `best` | the cheapest option found so far for this range |

narration.2: Remember the length of the array.
narration.4: Build the table with one spare row so ranges past the end read as empty (0 moves).
narration.6: Go from the last start position backwards so every shorter range to the right is already solved.
narration.7: Extend the range to the right one end position at a time.
narration.8: Option 1: delete arr[i] by itself, then clear the rest.
narration.9: Option 2: two equal neighbours form a palindrome of length two...
narration.10: ...so they leave together in one move.
narration.12: Option 3: look for a later copy of arr[i] at least two places away.
narration.13: Only an equal value can share a move with arr[i].
narration.14: Clear the inside; its last move also takes arr[i] and arr[k]. Then clear what follows k.
narration.17: Store the cheapest option for this range.
narration.20: The whole array is the range from 0 to n - 1.
